ch09.anchor: then chairman of the CCP Central Politburo and of its Standing Committee
ch09.note: Xiang Zhongfa (1880–1931), the man this chapter is about. A Wuhan dockworker and boatman turned union organizer, he was raised up at the Party’s 1928 Sixth Congress to nominal head of the Party, a proletarian figurehead; real authority lay with Li Lisan, and then with the Moscow-backed Wang Ming group and the Comintern. Gu Shunzhang’s defection in April 1931 exposed him, and he was seized in Shanghai on June 22, 1931, and shot within days. Whether he broke under interrogation is the question the chapter weighs. The standard accounts, and the Party’s own later verdict (Deng Yingchao, 1988, endorsed by Chen Yun), hold that he confessed at once and gave up his comrades; a dissenting minority (Zhang Ji’en) argued the confession was a forgery. His arrest and execution are not in doubt; what the sources here contest is the extent of his betrayal.

ch09.anchor: Huang Mulan has told us a story
ch09.note: Huang Mulan (1907–2017), an underground Communist courier and liaison in early-1930s Shanghai, later a businesswoman in Hong Kong and, after 1949, a prisoner for many years before her rehabilitation. Her long life and her 2012 memoir made her a celebrated figure, marketed as the “most beautiful red agent.” Her account of Xiang Zhongfa’s capture — that she overheard it by chance in a café — is the version the author sets out to test in this chapter, and treats throughout as an interested, self-flattering source. Her portrait appears below.

ch09.anchor: saving of Zhou Enlai and Guan Xiangying
ch09.note: Guan Xiangying (1902–1946), a Manchu Communist and youth and labor organizer, later political commissar of the 120th Division of the Eighth Route Army. Here he is simply the imprisoned comrade Huang Mulan was tasked with helping to free.

ch09.anchor: a film at the Grand
ch09.note: The Grand Theatre (Da Guangming), a landmark cinema on Bubbling Well Road; its Art Deco building, remodeled in 1933 by the architect László Hudec, was among the grandest picture houses in East Asia.

ch09.anchor: a heroine in the mold of Hua Mulan
ch09.note: Hua Mulan, the legendary woman warrior of the old Ballad of Mulan, who disguised herself as a man to take her aged father’s place in the army. Huang Mulan’s given name, Mulan (慕兰, “admiring Mulan”), is drawn from her — the point of the wordplay in this passage.

ch09.anchor: as for *Dream of the Red Chamber*
ch09.note: Two of the great classical Chinese novels: Romance of the Three Kingdoms, a sweeping historical war epic, and Dream of the Red Chamber, an intimate novel of a declining gentry house and its doomed romance. Huang Mulan offers her taste for the martial epic over the domestic romance as proof of her “masculine” temper.

ch09.anchor: publicly announced by Dong Biwu
ch09.note: Dong Biwu (1886–1975), a founder of the Chinese Communist Party and a delegate to its First Congress in 1921; after 1949 he became a vice-chairman of the People’s Republic and, for a time, its acting head of state.

ch09.anchor: married Wan Xiyan
ch09.note: Wan Xiyan (1900–1928), a Communist organizer and propagandist, Huang Mulan’s second husband; he was killed in 1928 leading a peasant force against the town of Wan’an in Jiangxi.

ch09.anchor: was He Chang, a member of the Sixth Central Committee
ch09.note: He Chang (1906–1935), a Communist labor and military-political leader, Huang Mulan’s third husband; he died during the Long March.

ch09.anchor: Chen Zhigao invited me for coffee
ch09.note: Chen Zhigao, a Shanghai lawyer and the son of a judge of the Mixed Court, who used his father’s name and his own connections to win the release of arrested comrades, and who later married Huang Mulan.

ch09.anchor: a student at Aurora University in Shanghai
ch09.note: The Université l’Aurore (Zhendan), a French Jesuit university in Shanghai’s French Concession, known for its law and medical faculties.

ch09.anchor: the North China Political Security Bureau
ch09.note: The Communist clandestine security and counter-intelligence network in the Beiping–Tianjin region, set up by Chen Geng after the Shanghai apparatus was blown. (Beiping was the name of Beijing from 1928 to 1949.)

ch09.anchor: the "Moskvin" of the Comintern department's report
ch09.note: “Moskvin” was Zhou Enlai’s codename in his dealings with the Comintern; the report’s reference to “Comrade Mo(skvin)” directing the reorganized special-work apparatus is thus a veiled naming of Zhou himself.

ch09.anchor: the Metropole Hotel and lie low for a time
ch09.note: The Metropole Hotel (Ducheng Fandian), a foreign-run hotel; the leaders’ brazen arrival in business dress, as the account has it, was itself the cover.

ch09.anchor: No. 44 Yong'anli on North Sichuan Road
ch09.note: A shikumen lane house in Hongkou used as one of Zhou Enlai’s Shanghai safe houses, now preserved as a memorial to his underground years. The author cites its later designation to press his point that Zhou would not still have been living there sixteen hours after Xiang’s arrest.

ch09.anchor: through Bao Wenwei, Wu Xingya
ch09.note: Bao Wenwei (1902–1991), a scholar of French literature who, under Special Branch direction, penetrated the Songhu Garrison Command as its French interpreter; he later became a university professor and the Chinese translator of Rabelais. His family’s account and Pan Hannian’s differ on the dates of his service, a discrepancy the author probes at length here.

ch09.anchor: his mother He Xiangning
ch09.note: He Xiangning (1878–1972), a revolutionary, painter, and widow of the Nationalist leader Liao Zhongkai; her son Liao Chengzhi (1908–1983), a Communist jailed at various times by both sides, rose after 1949 to senior posts in overseas-Chinese and foreign affairs.

ch09.anchor: the Hanyeping Company's ship No. 180
ch09.note: The Han-Ye-Ping Coal and Iron Company — the Hanyang ironworks, the Daye iron mines, and the Pingxiang colliery combined — was China’s first large modern iron-and-steel enterprise, centered on the Wuhan region where Xiang Zhongfa began as a worker.

ch09.anchor: the great Jinghan Railway workers' strike
ch09.note: The February 1923 strike on the Beijing–Hankou (Jinghan) Railway, crushed by the warlord Wu Peifu in the “February Seventh Massacre,” was a landmark and a bloody defeat for the early Communist-led labor movement.

ch09.anchor: Luo Zhanglong describes the Sixth Congress
ch09.note: Luo Zhanglong (1896–1995), one of the earliest Communist labor leaders; he broke with the leadership over the Fourth Plenum of 1931 and was expelled, which colors his memoir of these years.

ch09.anchor: Mif took his place
ch09.note: Pavel Mif, a Comintern official and rector of Sun Yat-sen University in Moscow, was the patron of Wang Ming and the Moscow-trained “Returned Students” (the “Twenty-eight Bolsheviks”). Luo Zhanglong’s account shows him installing Xiang Zhongfa as Party Secretary on Stalin’s instructions, to visibly muted applause.

ch09.anchor: those stood for the two most fashionable cuts
ch09.note: The joke turns on the shop-sign words Su-Guang-Cheng: Su for Suzhou, Guang for Guangdong (Canton), chengyi for ready-made clothes. “Suguangcheng” is not one shop’s name but the generic label “Suzhou-and-Cantonese tailoring,” so it hangs on more signboards than any other — which is also why the sources cannot agree whether Xiang’s safe house was the Suguangcheng grain shop or the Suguangcheng tailor shop.

ch09.anchor: Yang Hu, to negotiate
ch09.note: Yang Hu (1889–1966), a Green Gang-connected Nationalist general and Shanghai garrison commander, a principal enforcer of Chiang Kai-shek’s April 1927 purge of the Communists in the city.

ch09.anchor: then at Mount Lu, received the first urgent telegram
ch09.note: Mount Lu (Lushan) in Jiangxi, a cool highland resort that served as Chiang Kai-shek’s summer headquarters; from here he directed the Encirclement campaigns against the Communist base areas.

ch09.anchor: Kuomintang Zhongtong publication *The Turn* carries
ch09.note: The Turn (Zhuanbian) was an internal Zhongtong compilation of recantations by Communist defectors. The “Report of the Former Bogus CCP General Secretary Xiang Zhongfa” in its appendix — his so-called Confession — is the disputed document at the center of this chapter’s argument.

ch09.anchor: the Youth League General Secretary Qin Bangxian
ch09.note: Qin Bangxian (1907–1946), better known as Bo Gu, one of the Moscow-trained “Twenty-eight Bolsheviks”; within months he would head the Party’s Provisional Center.

ch09.anchor: Volume Eleven of the *Shilüe Gaoben*
ch09.note: The Shilüe Gaoben (Draft Chronicle) is the vast day-by-day compilation drawn from Chiang Kai-shek’s papers and diaries. The author’s discovery there of Chiang’s June 23 telegram ordering Xiang Zhongfa shot is the chapter’s clinching evidence: the “secret cable” whose very existence the section title disputes did, corroborated in Chiang’s own record, exist.
